narrative:
The model estimates a 71% chance that you will leave your current job, which is why your promotion request has been denied. This prediction is driven primarily by three key aspects of your professional background.

Your total years of experience across all roles stands out as the strongest factor pushing the model toward expecting you to leave. With 6–10 years overall, you fall into a mid-career range where many employees begin exploring new opportunities, unlike the majority of those predicted to stay, who tend to have only 1–5 years of total experience.

The second most influential factor is the time you have spent in your current organization. Having been there for 1–5 years places you in a period when people often evaluate whether to commit long-term or seek advancement elsewhere. This again contrasts with many employees the model sees as likely to stay, who typically have either much shorter or significantly longer tenure here.

Finally, the absence of other job offers you have received while working here actually pulls the prediction slightly back toward staying. Most employees the model expects to remain also report no external offers, so this factor provides a modest stabilizing influence.

Taken together, your mid-level experience and relatively short time in this role outweigh the positive signal from limited external opportunities, leading to the decision against promotion. The organization should discuss retention strategies with you, such as clearer promotion paths or enhanced support, while you may wish to reflect on your long-term career goals within or beyond this company.
